questions.stem: What is „Denglisch“?
options: German mixed with borrowed English words
A dialect spoken near the Danish border
The German taught to foreigners
An older spelling system
questions.explanation: „Denglisch“ blends Deutsch and Englisch. Words like „downloaden“ and „das Meeting“ are common in business and advertising, and are argued about in Germany much as Americanisms are in Britain.

questions.stem: What was the „Rechtschreibreform“ of 1996?
options: A reform of the school curriculum
The reunification of East and West German dictionaries
An official reform of German spelling
A law making German the official language
questions.explanation: The spelling reform changed rules on ß and ss among other things, and was unpopular enough that some newspapers refused to adopt it. It shows that spelling is decided by institutions, not by nature.

questions.stem: Which country has German as one of four official languages?
options: Liechtenstein
Switzerland
Austria
Belgium
questions.explanation: Switzerland's official languages are German, French, Italian and Romansh. Most Swiss German speakers use Swiss German dialects in speech and Standard German in writing.

questions.stem: What is „Schweizerdeutsch“?
options: A formal register used in Swiss government
An older form of German preserved in Switzerland
A group of spoken Swiss dialects, quite different from Standard German
The German taught in Swiss schools
questions.explanation: Swiss German is spoken everywhere in daily life but rarely written; Standard German is used for writing and formal broadcasting. Germans often need subtitles for Swiss German on television.

questions.stem: Why does German capitalise all nouns while English does not?
options: It was introduced by the 1996 spelling reform
Only German has nouns that can begin a sentence
It is a convention German kept and English gradually dropped
German nouns need capitals to show their gender
questions.explanation: English capitalised many nouns in the seventeenth century and stopped. German kept the habit and codified it, which is why it now looks like a German peculiarity rather than a shared inheritance.

questions.stem: Why does being invited to „duzen“ someone matter socially?
options: It means you must now use their surname
It applies only to people younger than you
It marks a shift from formal to familiar, and is usually offered explicitly
It is a grammatical correction
questions.explanation: The switch from „Sie“ to „du“ is often proposed by the older or senior person, sometimes with a drink. English lost the distinction with 'thou' and now signals closeness through names and tone instead.

questions.stem: What does „das Duzen“ and „das Siezen“ show about German?
options: Both words mean the same thing
A verb can be made from a pronoun and turned into a noun
Pronouns change with the seasons
German has no formal address in writing
questions.explanation: German freely turns other words into nouns — any infinitive can become „das …“ — so the act of saying „du“ to someone has its own name. English needs a whole phrase for the same idea.

questions.stem: Why is „der Handschuh“ a good example of how German builds words?
options: It is borrowed from English
It has no gender
It is an old word no longer used
It joins Hand and Schuh into one word meaning glove
questions.explanation: German compounds freely, and the last element sets the gender — „der Schuh“ makes „der Handschuh“. Its famously long words are usually three ordinary nouns joined up.

questions.stem: What is „Hochdeutsch“ in relation to dialects?
options: The only correct form of German
A polite register used with strangers
The written and broadcast standard, alongside strong regional dialects
The dialect spoken in the mountains
questions.explanation: Standard German coexists with Bavarian, Swabian, Plattdeutsch and others. Speakers move between them, and dialect is often a marker of where you are from rather than of education.

questions.stem: Why does German need cases where English mostly manages without?
options: English lost its cases in the twentieth century
Cases mark each word's role, which frees the word order to move
German has no fixed word order at all
Cases exist only in formal writing
questions.explanation: English fixes roles by position — 'the dog bites the man'. German marks them on the article, so a phrase can move to the front for emphasis without anyone losing track of who did what.

questions.stem: Why might „Ich will einen Kaffee“ sound abrupt to a German speaker?
options: „Wollen“ states a want directly where a softer form is expected
It uses the wrong case for „Kaffee“
The word order is incorrect
„Kaffee“ is the wrong gender
questions.explanation: „Ich hätte gern“ or „ich möchte“ soften the request. The sentence is grammatically perfect, which is exactly why grammar alone will not tell you it lands badly.

questions.stem: What do the flavouring particles „doch“, „mal“ and „eben“ do?
options: They are required in every sentence
They carry tone rather than meaning
They mark the past tense
They make a sentence negative
questions.explanation: „Komm mal her“ and „komm doch her“ differ in attitude, not content. English does this job with intonation, which is why the particles are hard to translate and easy to leave out.

questions.stem: What does the existence of „der Computer“ alongside „der Rechner“ show?
options: Older words always replace newer ones
A language can borrow a word and keep a native one alongside it
German never borrows from English
Technical terms must be translated by law
questions.explanation: „Rechner“ is built from „rechnen“, to calculate. Both are in use, with „Computer“ more common in speech — two words for one thing, and speakers choosing between them.

questions.stem: Why is cultural context needed to read a German text, not just vocabulary?
options: Meaning depends on shared references a dictionary does not carry
German grammar changes by region
German texts rarely state their subject
Vocabulary cannot be looked up
questions.explanation: A reference to „das Abitur“ or „die Wende“ carries weight for a German reader that a translation flattens. This is what UL04 means by identity shaping ways of communicating.

questions.stem: What does it mean that German is a pluricentric language?
options: It has more than one alphabet
It has a formal and an informal register
Germany, Austria and Switzerland each have an accepted standard form
It is spoken on several continents
questions.explanation: An Austrian says „Jänner“ where a German says „Januar“, and neither is wrong. English is pluricentric in the same way, which is why Australian English is not incorrect British English.

questions.stem: What is „die Wende“?
options: A spelling reform of the 1990s
The name of the German parliament
The period of change around German reunification in 1989–90
A regional dialect of eastern Germany
questions.explanation: „Die Wende“ means the turning point. It is the word Germans use for the fall of the Berlin Wall and what followed, and it appears constantly in Year 10 texts about recent German history.

questions.stem: Which countries have German as an official language?
options: Germany, Austria and Switzerland
Germany and Poland only
Germany and the Netherlands
Germany and Denmark
questions.explanation: German is official in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and parts of Belgium and Italy. Switzerland has four official languages in all.

questions.stem: What is the Bundesland?
options: The German national anthem
A federal state within Germany
The national parliament
A type of regional dialect
questions.explanation: Germany has sixteen Bundesländer, each with its own government and its own school system. That is why school holidays differ across the country.

questions.stem: What is the Abitur?
options: The qualification for university entry
A national sporting competition
A type of apprenticeship
The school leaving age
questions.explanation: The Abitur is taken at the end of the Gymnasium and is the usual route to university. The Ausbildung is the apprenticeship route instead.

questions.stem: What is an Ausbildung?
options: A final examination taken at the end of school
A year spent abroad between school and work
A degree course taken at a German university
A paid apprenticeship combining work and study
questions.explanation: The dual system splits the week between a company and a vocational school, and it is a respected path rather than a fallback. It is one of the clearest differences from Australian schooling.

questions.stem: Why is the formal "Sie" used more in German than "vous" in some other languages?
options: It is the only form taught in schools
It is used only with older people
It is required by law in business
It marks respect and distance in most public settings
questions.explanation: Germans typically use Sie with anyone they do not know, including colleagues, until du is offered. Switching too early can seem presumptuous.

questions.stem: What is Fasching or Karneval?
options: A national day of remembrance
A festival before Lent with parades and costumes
A summer music festival
A harvest celebration in autumn
questions.explanation: It is strongest in the Rhineland, especially Cologne, and peaks on Rosenmontag. Regional differences in its name and scale are part of the point.

questions.stem: What is the Oktoberfest and where is it held?
options: A festival in Berlin held in October
A wine festival on the Rhine
A Christmas market in Nuremberg
A festival in Munich that begins in September
questions.explanation: Despite the name it starts in September and runs into early October, and it is held in Munich, in Bavaria. Australians often assume it is nationwide, but it is strongly Bavarian.

questions.stem: What does the Berlin Wall represent in modern German identity?
options: The division and later reunification of the country
A defence against invasion from the west
A boundary between two language regions
A monument built after reunification
questions.explanation: It stood from 1961 to 1989 and separated East from West Berlin. Its fall is commemorated annually, and reunification remains a live topic.

questions.stem: What is a Weihnachtsmarkt?
options: A Christmas market in a town square
A New Year fireworks display
A spring flower festival
A summer street fair
questions.explanation: They run through Advent and sell food, drink and crafts, with Glühwein and Lebkuchen the most familiar. Nuremberg and Dresden hold the best known.

questions.stem: What is typically eaten as the main meal in Germany, and when?
options: A large breakfast only
A hot meal at midday
A hot meal in the evening
A cold meal at midday
questions.explanation: Mittagessen has traditionally been the main hot meal, with Abendbrot a lighter cold supper. Working patterns are changing this, but the words still reflect it.

questions.stem: What does "Duzen" mean?
options: Introducing two strangers
Ending a conversation politely
Using the informal du with someone
Greeting someone formally
questions.explanation: Duzen and siezen are verbs for which form of address you use. Being invited to duzen someone is a small social milestone.

questions.stem: What is the Bundeskanzler?
options: The head of state
The mayor of Berlin
The president of the parliament
The head of the German government
questions.explanation: The Chancellor leads the government while the Bundespräsident is head of state with a largely ceremonial role. The split is a deliberate feature of the constitution.

questions.stem: What is the Autobahn known for?
options: Sections with no general speed limit
Being toll roads for all vehicles
Being limited to commercial traffic
Running only between major cities
questions.explanation: Many stretches have an advisory limit rather than a legal one, though limits apply in roadworks and urban areas. It is often overstated abroad.

questions.stem: Why does Switzerland have four official languages?
options: Each canton chose a language by vote
Its regions historically spoke different languages
It was divided after a war
It adopted the languages of its neighbours by treaty
questions.explanation: German, French, Italian and Romansh reflect the long-standing linguistic regions. Swiss German itself differs enough from standard German to need subtitles on television.

questions.stem: What is recycling like in Germany?
options: Only paper is recycled
Waste is sorted into several separate bins
All waste goes into one bin
Recycling is voluntary and rare
questions.explanation: Household waste is separated by type, and drink containers carry a Pfand deposit returned at the shop. Environmental practice is a common speaking topic.

questions.stem: What is Pfand?
options: A deposit paid on a bottle and refunded on return
A tax added to goods imported from abroad
A tip left for staff at the end of a meal
A fine issued for dropping litter in public
questions.explanation: The deposit gives bottles a cash value, which is why collection is so high. Machines in supermarkets take the containers and print a voucher.

questions.stem: What is the Mauerfall and why does it matter?
options: The rebuilding of central Berlin during the 1950s and 1960s
The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, which led to reunification
The building of the Berlin Wall in 1961, which divided the city
The treaty signed in 1945 that ended the war in Europe
questions.explanation: The wall opened on 9 November 1989 and Germany reunified less than a year later. It is the single most referenced event in modern German culture.

questions.stem: How do Germans usually greet someone in a shop?
options: Wie geht es dir, asked of every stranger
Auf Wiedersehen, said when entering
Guten Tag, or Grüß Gott in the south
Hallo Freund, used with anyone you meet
questions.explanation: A greeting on entering is expected and its absence is noticed. Grüß Gott is standard in Bavaria and Austria.

questions.stem: What is a Gymnasium in the German school system?
options: A primary school for younger children
A university department
An academic secondary school leading to the Abitur
A sports hall attached to a school
questions.explanation: It is one of several secondary school types, and the false friend with the English gymnasium catches most learners once.

questions.stem: Why do German shops close on Sundays?
options: Local councils decide each week
Laws restrict Sunday trading
There is no demand for it
Staff shortages prevent it
questions.explanation: The Ladenschlussgesetz restricts Sunday opening, with limited exceptions for stations and petrol stations. It surprises visitors used to seven-day trading.

questions.stem: What language is spoken in Austria?
options: German, with its own words and accent
Austrian, a separate language
Mostly Hungarian
German only in the cities
questions.explanation: Austrian German differs in vocabulary and pronunciation, so Jänner is used rather than Januar. It is a variety of German, not a separate language.

questions.stem: What does the Pfand system suggest about German attitudes to waste?
options: Reuse is built into everyday habits
Waste is mainly a council responsibility
Recycling is seen as optional
Packaging is rarely used
questions.explanation: Attaching money to a container makes returning it the normal thing to do rather than an effort. Environmental questions often ask what a practice reveals about values.

questions.stem: What does it mean that a language has 'register'?
options: It offers levels of formality for the same idea
It keeps a record of every new word coined
It has one fixed written form and no other
It is spoken officially in several countries
questions.explanation: „Gib mir“, „Ich möchte“ and „Könnten Sie mir bitte“ ask for the same thing at three social distances.

questions.stem: Which is the most formal way to ask for something in German?
options: Ich brauche Hilfe
Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
Kannst du mir helfen?
Hilf mir mal
questions.explanation: The conditional of „können“ with „Sie“ and „bitte“ is the top of the scale. The imperative is the bottom.

questions.stem: What does switching from „Sie“ to „du“ usually require?
options: Permission from a third person present
An invitation from the older or senior person
A written agreement between the two people
A minimum of one year of acquaintance
questions.explanation: It is a small social ceremony rather than a grammar choice, and taking it uninvited reads as presumption.

questions.stem: What does „Denglisch“ describe?
options: German mixed with English borrowings
German taught to English speakers
A dialect spoken near the Danish border
The German used in British newspapers
questions.explanation: „Downloaden“ and „gecancelt“ take English stems and German endings. Critics dislike it; speakers keep using it.

questions.stem: How does German usually adapt a borrowed English verb?
options: It turns the verb into a compound noun
It adds German endings to the English stem
It translates each part into German
It leaves the verb entirely unchanged
questions.explanation: „Ich habe gegoogelt“ takes the participle pattern. Once that happens the word behaves as German.

questions.stem: What gender does a borrowed English noun take in German?
options: The speaker chooses freshly each time
One is assigned, often by analogy
It has no gender at all
It is always neuter without exception
questions.explanation: „Das Handy“ and „die E-Mail“ each got a gender. German has no slot for a noun without one.

questions.stem: Why do some German speakers object to Denglisch?
options: Borrowing is forbidden by German law
They see it as crowding out German words
They find English words harder to spell
Borrowed words cannot take German endings
questions.explanation: The objection is cultural rather than grammatical. German has borrowed from Latin and French for centuries.

questions.stem: What was the 1996 Rechtschreibreform?
options: A treaty on language between three countries
A revision of German spelling rules
A law requiring German in advertising
A change to the German school calendar
questions.explanation: It changed ß and ss usage, among other things, and was contested enough that some newspapers refused it for years.

questions.stem: Why was the spelling reform controversial?
options: People were attached to the spellings they had learnt
It made German harder to pronounce correctly
It removed the umlauts from the alphabet
It applied only in Austria and Switzerland
questions.explanation: Spelling carries identity. The same argument surfaces whenever English reform is proposed.

questions.stem: What does it mean that Swiss German is a spoken variety?
options: It is used only in official Swiss documents
It is used in speech while standard German is written
It has no speakers left under forty
It is a separate language from German entirely
questions.explanation: A learner can read every Swiss newspaper and still not follow two Swiss people talking to each other.

questions.stem: Which is an Austrian word where Germany says „Kartoffel“?
options: Apfelbaum
Kartoffelbrot
Erdapfel
Erdnuss
questions.explanation: Literally 'earth apple', the same image as French « pomme de terre ». Food vocabulary varies most between the standards.

questions.stem: Which is the Austrian word for January?
options: Erstmonat
Jänner
Januar
Jahresanfang
questions.explanation: Austria writes „Jänner“ where Germany writes „Januar“. Both are standard in their own country.

questions.stem: What does it mean that German is pluricentric in practice?
options: One country decides the standard for all of them
The written forms are identical everywhere
Only Germany has a recognised standard form
Each country's standard is correct in its own place
questions.explanation: Austrian German is not deviant German. The same is true of Australian against British English.

questions.stem: What does compounding let German do that English does with phrases?
options: Show the gender of every noun clearly
Mark which words are borrowed
Build one precise word from several shorter ones
Avoid using prepositions in a sentence
questions.explanation: „Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung“ is a speed limit. English would use three words and mean the same thing.

questions.stem: Why do German compounds look intimidating to learners?
options: The parts change their spelling completely
They take a different gender from their parts
They can only be used in formal writing
The parts are joined with no spaces between them
questions.explanation: Split „Handschuh“ into hand and shoe and it stops being frightening. The last part gives the gender.

questions.stem: What does „Schadenfreude“ show about borrowing?
options: English cannot form its own compound words
Borrowed words never keep their original sense
English takes words for ideas it has no term for
German words are always longer than English ones
questions.explanation: English had the feeling and no compact word for it, so it took the German one whole.

questions.stem: What does „Zeitgeist“ mean?
options: A newspaper published weekly
The spirit of a particular time
A measurement of elapsed time
A ghost story from folklore
questions.explanation: Time plus spirit. English borrowed it for exactly the reason it borrowed „Schadenfreude“.

questions.stem: What does „Weltanschauung“ describe?
options: An international news programme
A comprehensive view of the world
A famous viewpoint over a valley
A world championship in a sport
questions.explanation: World plus view. Philosophy borrowed it because 'worldview' arrived later and carries less weight.

questions.stem: Why do English and German share basic vocabulary?
options: German borrowed the words from English
The two were a single language until 1500
Both descend from a common Germanic ancestor
English borrowed the words in the last century
questions.explanation: Hand, water, house and come are inherited rather than borrowed, which is why they are the plainest words in both.

questions.stem: What is a false friend?
options: A word borrowed and then given back
A word with two accepted spellings
A word that looks familiar and means something else
A word that cannot be translated at all
questions.explanation: „Gift“ means poison and „bekommen“ means receive. The resemblance is exactly what makes them dangerous.

questions.stem: What does the false friend „Gymnasium“ mean?
options: A university department
A public swimming pool
An academic secondary school
A hall used for sport
questions.explanation: Sport happens in „die Turnhalle“. The English sense came from the same Greek root by a different route.

questions.stem: What does „aktuell“ mean?
options: Current or up to date
Actual, as opposed to imagined
Accurate to the last detail
Eventually, after some delay
questions.explanation: 'Actually' is „eigentlich“. French « actuellement » sets the same trap.

questions.stem: What does „sensibel“ mean in German?
options: Able to be sensed or measured
Reasonable in price
Sensitive to things around you
Sensible and level-headed
questions.explanation: 'Sensible' in English is „vernünftig“. The pair catches learners going both ways.

questions.stem: Why is literal translation often inadequate?
options: Words have different numbers of letters
Grammar works identically in both languages
Dictionaries leave out the common words
Idiom and connotation do not cross word for word
questions.explanation: „Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof“ is 'I only understand station' and means 'this is all Greek to me'.

questions.stem: What does „Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof“ mean?
options: I have no idea what is being said
I am waiting at the railway station
I understand only the simplest German
I would rather travel by train
questions.explanation: Knowing every word in the idiom gets you nowhere near the meaning, which is what makes idiom worth studying separately.

questions.stem: What does „Tomaten auf den Augen haben“ mean?
options: To be crying about a small problem
To be short-sighted and need glasses
To miss something obvious in front of you
To be growing vegetables at home
questions.explanation: Literally 'to have tomatoes on your eyes'. English says you cannot see what is under your nose.

questions.stem: What does „Jugendsprache“ refer to?
options: An older form of written German
The language of young people
The German taught in primary schools
The formal register used in courts
questions.explanation: Publishers pick a word of the year for it. Once adults adopt a term, the group usually moves on.

questions.stem: Why does youth slang change quickly?
options: It follows no grammatical rules at all
It is chosen by publishers each year
It marks a group, so it renews as it spreads
It is never written down anywhere
questions.explanation: The moment a term is understood by everyone it stops doing its job, so the group replaces it.

questions.stem: What does code-switching describe?
options: Learning two languages in the same year
Writing German using an English keyboard
Moving between languages within one conversation
Translating a written document carefully
questions.explanation: It takes fluent control of both grammars, which is why monolingual speakers cannot do it.

questions.stem: Why is code-switching a sign of skill rather than confusion?
options: It happens only when speaking slowly
It replaces grammar with gesture and tone
It occurs only in written communication
It requires the grammar of both languages at once
questions.explanation: Switching at the wrong point produces something neither language accepts, so the switch points have to be judged.

questions.stem: What does 'language contact' produce?
options: A complete loss of grammar in both languages
A translation of one language into another
Borrowing and new varieties where speakers meet
A single language replacing all the others
questions.explanation: German has taken from Latin, French and now English, and has given words back in each direction.

questions.stem: Which statement about German dialect and standard is accurate?
options: Many speakers use both, choosing by situation
Dialect speakers cannot use the standard form
The standard has entirely replaced dialect
Dialects are simplified versions of the standard
questions.explanation: Switching between dialect at home and standard at work is ordinary, not a sign of poor German.

questions.stem: Why is Low German sometimes called a separate language?
options: It differs from standard German more than a dialect would
It is spoken outside Germany only
It has no relationship to standard German
It was created after the Second World War
questions.explanation: „Plattdeutsch“ is recognised as a regional language in Germany, and the dialect-or-language line is often political.

questions.stem: What decides whether a variety counts as a language or a dialect?
options: How old the variety can be shown to be
Political recognition as much as linguistic distance
The number of speakers it currently has
Whether it has a written alphabet
questions.explanation: Mutually unintelligible varieties are called dialects of Chinese; mutually intelligible ones are called Swedish and Norwegian.

questions.stem: Why might a German speaker seem blunt to an Australian?
options: Directness is valued as honesty in German conversation
German lacks any polite forms of address
German has no equivalent of the word please
German speakers avoid eye contact when talking
questions.explanation: The language has a full politeness system. The difference is in what counts as considerate.

questions.stem: What does „Termin“ mean?
options: A deadline that cannot be moved
An appointment at a set time
The end of a period of study
A term used in a technical field
questions.explanation: „Einen Termin machen“ is to make an appointment. The English 'term' is a false friend hiding in it.

questions.stem: What does the phrase „Ordnung muss sein“ express?
options: A warning given before an exam
A cultural value placed on order
A legal requirement about public space
A greeting used in the workplace
questions.explanation: It is half proverb and half joke about German self-image, which is part of why it is quoted so often.

questions.stem: What is „die Duzkultur“ in some German companies?
options: A workplace where everyone uses du
A training course in formal address
A rule that bans first names at work
A yearly staff social event
questions.explanation: Tech firms and start-ups often adopt it deliberately, which is itself a statement about hierarchy.

questions.stem: Why does German have gendered job titles like „Lehrerin“?
options: The language marks gender on many person nouns
The suffix marks which subject is taught
It distinguishes trained from untrained staff
It was introduced to replace the masculine form
questions.explanation: The -in suffix is regular and productive, so almost any role can take a feminine form.

questions.stem: What is „das Gendersternchen“ used for?
options: Showing that a word has been borrowed
Indicating the stress in a long word
Writing a job title to include all genders
Marking a footnote in academic writing
questions.explanation: „Lehrer*innen“ is one solution among several, and the debate about it is about who the language makes visible.

questions.stem: Why do debates about inclusive language get heated?
options: The rules change every year in any case
Grammar choices carry claims about who counts
Changing grammar makes a language harder to learn
Only a government can alter a language officially
questions.explanation: The argument is rarely about grammar itself. It is about what the grammar is taken to say.

questions.stem: What does it mean that German uses „man“ where English uses a passive?
options: Man is the formal version of the passive
An active verb with a vague subject does the job
German has no passive construction at all
The passive is reserved for written German
questions.explanation: „Man sagt“ rather than 'it is said'. Both leave the speaker unnamed, by different routes.

questions.stem: Why is German useful for reading older scientific work?
options: German is the official language of science
Much research was published in German before 1940
Scientific terms cannot be translated from German
Journals still require a German summary
questions.explanation: Physics and chemistry in particular have a large German-language literature from that period.

questions.stem: What does the survival of German place names in South Australia show?
options: The names were translated from local languages
The names were chosen by the British government
Settlers brought the language with them
German was once an official state language
questions.explanation: Hahndorf and Lobethal date from 1830s Lutheran settlement. Some names were changed during the First World War and later restored.

questions.stem: Why were some German place names changed in Australia in 1918?
options: A request from the German government
Confusion with similar names elsewhere
Anti-German feeling during the First World War
A national policy of standardising spelling
questions.explanation: Language and politics rarely stay separate. Several were restored decades later.

questions.stem: What does learning German tend to reveal about English?
options: Choices English makes that go unnoticed
That English grammar is simpler throughout
That English has fewer words available
That English was derived from German
questions.explanation: Meeting cases and verb-second makes you notice that English relies on word order to do the same work.

questions.stem: Why is word order more flexible in German than English?
options: German sentences are usually shorter
German has no rules about word order
Verbs can be left out of a sentence
Case endings show who is doing what
questions.explanation: „Den Hund sieht der Mann“ still means the man sees the dog. English has to keep the subject first.

questions.stem: What does an interpreter have to carry across besides the words?
options: Register, idiom and what the speaker intends
The exact number of words in each sentence
The speaker's accent and speaking speed
The grammar of the original language
questions.explanation: Right words and wrong register turns a polite request into an order.

questions.stem: What does subtitling sacrifice compared with the original?
options: The whole meaning of the spoken dialogue
The sequence in which events happen
The identity of the character speaking
Some nuance, because the text must stay brief
questions.explanation: Reading speed limits how much can be shown, so subtitles compress. Dubbing keeps the words and loses the performance.

questions.stem: Why do some German films keep their titles abroad?
options: The title carries a tone translation would lose
Film titles cannot legally be translated
Distributors save money by not translating
German titles are always shorter than English
questions.explanation: „Das Boot“ travelled untranslated. Sometimes the foreignness is part of what is being sold.

questions.stem: What does the variety of German across three countries suggest?
options: Languages change as the communities using them change
Languages get simpler the longer they are spoken
Standards are fixed permanently by dictionaries
Neighbouring languages eventually merge into one
questions.explanation: Variation is the normal state of a living language. A single unchanging standard has to be actively maintained.
